title: CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. (June 2013 TCC) Decision
subject: Wireless communications company SR&ED appeal involving hardware and firmware development expenditure eligibility.
summary: In CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 201, the Tax Court of Canada held that a $1,990,036 one-time bonus paid to SR&ED employees after the sale of Dataradio was not an eligible SR&ED salary expenditure under the proxy method. For Canadian claimants, bonuses tied to an acquisition, not the prosecution of SR&ED, are disallowed.
metaDescription: Examine the June 2013 Tax Court of Canada ruling for CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. concerning Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
1.1 Corporate Context and the Taxpayer's SR&ED Claim

In CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 201 (Docket: 2010-3708(IT)G), handed down on June 25, 2013, the Tax Court of Canada addressed a foundational question in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax law: whether a one-time bonus incentive paid to technical employees following an acquisition of control qualifies as an allowable SR&ED expenditure under the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"). The appellant, CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. (the corporation resulting from the May 30, 2006 amalgamation of Dataradio Inc. ("Old Dataradio") with 4352491 Canada Inc., which continued under the name Dataradio Inc. until February 5, 2010; Old Dataradio was headquartered in Metropolitan Montreal, Quebec, and was a Canadian-controlled private corporation until May 10, 2006), operated in the designing, manufacturing, marketing and selling of wireless data products for fixed and mobile applications. On May 9, 2006, CalAmp Corp., a Delaware corporation headquartered in California whose shares are traded on NASDAQ, acquired all of the outstanding shares of Old Dataradio through its wholly-owned subsidiary 4308093 Canada Inc. for USD$54,291,000 (approximately CAD$60.1 million); in connection with this sale, approximately CAD$5,900,000 was allocated to bonuses for several categories of Old Dataradio's workforce (not only SR&ED employees), of which $1,990,036 was paid, no earlier than June 23, 2006, to the employees engaged in SR&ED in Canada during the short taxation year from March 1 to May 9, 2006 (the period at issue).

In filing its corporate income tax return and prescribed Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), the appellant included the portion of this one-time bonus paid to its R&D workforce within its pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA and its qualified expenditures for calculating Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under subsections 127(5) and 127(9). Specifically, having elected the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA (an election filed in accordance with subsection 37(10)), the taxpayer included the $1,990,036 in bonuses within the $2,589,681 of salaries declared for its SR&ED employees under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) of the ITA, contending that the bonuses constituted "salary or wages" as defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA that were taxable in the employees' hands, that they were paid to non-specified employees because those employees were performing SR&ED, and that, because subsection 37(9) of the ITA excludes only bonuses paid to specified employees, Parliament did not intend to exclude bonuses paid to other employees.
1.2 The Minister's Challenge and Administrative Position

The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), by Notice of Assessment dated February 25, 2009 (confirmed by Notice of Confirmation dated September 17, 2010), assessed the appellant for the taxation year ending May 9, 2006 to reduce its initially claimed refundable ITC of $302,973 by $131,260, on the basis that the $1,990,036 in bonuses paid to its SR&ED employees did not constitute an expenditure of SR&ED directly undertaken by the appellant and did not constitute a qualified expenditure. Notably, the eligibility of the fourteen SR&ED projects declared for the period (involving fifteen scientists and engineers, twenty-two technologists and technicians, five managers and administrators, and one technical support staff member) was not the subject of the appeal; in every other respect the assessment was a nil assessment, and the Court identified the only issue as whether there was a reasonable connection between the bonus incentives and the prosecution of SR&ED.

Rather, the Crown challenged the legal and factual nexus between the one-time bonus expenditure and the actual performance of SR&ED. The Minister's position rested on the statutory requirement that for remuneration to qualify as an SR&ED expenditure under subsection 37(1) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) (specifically subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), the provision applicable under the proxy method elected by the appellant) of the ITA, it is insufficient for a payment merely to fall within the broad baseline definition of taxable employment income under section 5 and subsection 248(1) while being paid to an individual who happens to perform R&D. Instead, the Crown argued that the expenditure itself must be incurred "on" or "in respect of" the prosecution of SR&ED and must reasonably be considered to relate to the SR&ED work performed. Because the bonus incentives were tied to the sale of the company, were represented by management to the employees as a gift, gave the employees no legally enforceable right to require their payment, and were unrelated to the extent and nature of the SR&ED activities undertaken from March 1 to May 9, 2006, the Minister maintained that the payment lacked the requisite statutory link to SR&ED.
1.3 Governing Canadian Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. is governed by an interlocking series of provisions within the Income Tax Act (Canada) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (the "ITR"). At the foundation of the regime, subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines "scientific research and experimental development" as systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes. This statutory definition also encompasses enumerated support work—specifically engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research—where such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development. Simultaneously, subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines "salary or wages", except in sections 5 and 63 and the definition of "death benefit", as meaning the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA (sections 5 to 8), which, through section 5, includes salary, wages and other remuneration, including gratuities, received in the year, and which also includes fees for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business but does not include superannuation or pension benefits or retiring allowances.

While subsection 248(1) establishes the general definitions of SR&ED and salary or wages, paragraph 37(1)(a) of the ITA governs expenditure deductibility, permitting a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature made by the taxpayer in the year "on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer". This primary deduction rule is further circumscribed by subsection 37(8) of the ITA, which restricts which expenditures qualify as expenditures "on or in respect of scientific research and experimental development". Under the traditional overhead method governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), qualified expenditures include an expenditure of a current nature all or substantially all of which was attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or an expenditure of a current nature directly attributable, as determined by regulation, to that prosecution (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and paragraph 2900(2)(b) of the ITR), including salary or wages of an employee who is directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting the prosecution of SR&ED to the extent that the amount "can reasonably be considered to be in respect of such prosecution". Conversely, under the proxy method governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), where a taxpayer elects in prescribed form, eligible salary or wages are strictly restricted under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) to "that portion of an expenditure made in respect of an expense incurred in the year for salary or wages of an employee who is directly engaged in scientific research and experimental development in Canada that can reasonably be considered to relate to such work having regard to the time spent by the employee thereon" for an employee who is "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada.

Complementing subsection 37(8) of the ITA, subsections 2900(4) through 2900(9) of the ITR stipulate that a taxpayer electing the proxy method calculates a notional overhead amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—based on the eligible salary base of employees "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada, with subsection 2900(9) of the ITR excluding from that salary base, among other items, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits (whether or not paid to specified employees) and taxable benefits, while amounts for extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits, and retiring allowances are not treated as SR&ED salary or wages at all. Finally, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA grant SR&ED Investment Tax Credits as a percentage of a taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" pool, which incorporates eligible current SR&ED expenditures determined under subsection 37(1) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) or (B), augmented by the PPA calculated under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR.
1.4 Final Holding and Judicial Rationale of the Tax Court of Canada

The Tax Court of Canada dismissed the appeal of CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. and upheld the Minister's assessment, which reduced the appellant's initially claimed refundable ITC of $302,973 by $131,260 in respect of the bonuses. The Court held that no connection or link existed between the one-time bonus incentive paid to the appellant's SR&ED employees in connection with the sale of Old Dataradio and the prosecution of SR&ED activities during the taxation year at issue (March 1 to May 9, 2006).

In its judicial analysis, the Court held that, because the appellant had elected the proxy method, the only issue was whether the $1,990,036 constituted expenditures made in respect of an expense incurred in the appellant's 2006 taxation year for salary or wages within the meaning of subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) of the ITA, that is, whether there was a reasonable connection between the bonus incentives and the prosecution of SR&ED. First, the Court observed that the appellant's written submissions, which relied on the absence of any restriction on the length of a taxation year, the limited exclusion in subsection 37(9) for specified employees, the CRA's earlier interpretation letters, and the presumption in favour of the taxpayer, did not address that issue, and that the subclause clearly allows only that portion of salary and wages that can reasonably be considered to relate to SR&ED activities. Second, the Court held that whether any portion of a bonus relates to SR&ED in the year is a question of fact that requires determining the underlying reasons for paying the bonus, which must be distinguished from the method of calculating it (here, years of service, current salary and merit). The Court found that the bonuses were paid mainly because Old Dataradio's shareholder believed that salaried employees should share in the financial success resulting from the sale of the company, and because of the corresponding benefit to the purchaser of creating conditions favouring employee retention after the acquisition, even though the bonuses were not conditional on the employees staying with CalAmp Corp. The Court further noted that these payments stood in stark contrast to Old Dataradio's traditional policy of modest Christmas bonuses (one SR&ED employee received $24,242 in 2006, almost ten times any bonus he had previously received), that the appellant's president candidly admitted that the bonuses were not related to the prosecution of SR&ED activities during the two-month 2006 period, that the payment was an isolated event rather than a response to a recurrent need to compensate SR&ED employees (Alcatel Canada Inc. v. Canada, 2006 TCC 149), and that the appellant had not shown the expenditures to have a direct relationship with, and to be essential to the completion of, the research projects (Laboratoire Du-Var Inc. v. Canada, 2012 TCC 366). Consequently, even though the bonuses were paid to employees directly engaged in SR&ED, the absence of a reasonable connection between the bonuses and the prosecution of SR&ED in the taxation year meant that they did not qualify as SR&ED expenditures under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) of the ITA, and the appeal was dismissed (bonuses being, in any event, excluded from the proxy salary base under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR). The Court expressly noted that its analysis was consistent with the CRA's previously published SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (December 19, 2012), which states that there is no reasonable link to SR&ED where a bonus is paid out of income earned from a capital transaction such as the sale of the business or of shares; accordingly, CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 201 reflects, rather than created, the position set out in the CRA's administrative Salary or Wages Policy on bonuses funded by the proceeds of capital transactions.
2. Core Legal, Contractual, and Evidentiary Failures
2.1 Absence of Statutory Nexus: The "On or In Respect Of" Standard Under Subsection 37(1) and Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)

The primary legal failure in CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. stemmed from conflating the taxability of employment remuneration in the hands of the employee with the deductibility and creditability of that expenditure as SR&ED in the hands of the employer. Under section 5 and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, virtually any payment flowing from an employer to an employee by virtue of the employment relationship—including a signing bonus, a retention payment, or a post-acquisition incentive—is swept into "salary or wages". The appellant relied on this broad statutory definition to argue that once a payment is legally classified as "salary or wages" of an employee who is "directly engaged" in SR&ED, that payment qualifies as an SR&ED expenditure under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), relying in particular on CRA interpretation letters (No. 9320837 of November 26, 1993, and No. 96-06 of June 28, 1996) and on the fact that subsection 37(9) excludes only bonuses paid to specified employees.

The Tax Court dismantled this argument by focusing on the limiting language of subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), the provision applicable under the proxy method elected by the appellant, and by observing that the appellant's submissions did not address the only relevant issue. Under this provision, "salary or wages" are eligible only to the extent that the expenditure was made "on" or "in respect of" SR&ED and represents "that portion of an expenditure made in respect of an expense incurred in the year for salary or wages of an employee who is directly engaged in scientific research and experimental development in Canada that can reasonably be considered to relate to such work having regard to the time spent by the employee thereon". Under the statutory scheme, the words "such work" refer specifically to the hands-on activities of undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED (under the traditional method) or being "directly engaged in SR&ED" (under the proxy method). Because the bonuses were paid mainly so that salaried employees would share in the financial success resulting from the sale of the company and to favour employee retention for the purchaser, the Court found that the underlying reasons for the payment were connected to the share sale rather than to the performance of experimental development during the taxation year from March 1 to May 9, 2006, the only period relevant to the inquiry. Without a demonstrable functional link showing that the bonus was paid as consideration for carrying out experiments, testing hypotheses, or resolving technological uncertainties, the payment failed the statutory nexus requirement.
2.2 Contractual Characterization: Acquisition-Triggered Retention Inducements Versus Performance-Based SR&ED Remuneration

A critical evidentiary failure identified in the ruling—and consistent with the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy—was the character of the bonus itself: the bonuses were accrued as of the closing date under section 6.11 of the Share Purchase Agreement, were represented by management to the employees as a gift, and gave the SR&ED employees no legally enforceable right to require their payment. As highlighted in Canadian SR&ED commentary and administrative guidance analyzing CalAmp, "remuneration referred to as a bonus in an employment contract may not necessarily be a bonus" for SR&ED purposes if its substantive legal character is an inducement or a non-competition payment (which the CRA treats as regular salary or wages rather than as a bonus); the Court in CalAmp did not, however, decide the appeal on this characterization, but on the absence of a reasonable connection between the bonuses and the prosecution of SR&ED.

In the context of an acquisition of control, acquiring corporations frequently establish retention pools or transaction bonus plans to prevent key technical personnel from departing during the post-closing transition period. However, in CalAmp, the bonuses were accrued as of the closing date of the share sale and, although section 6.5 of the Share Purchase Agreement stated the purchaser's intention to continue the employment of all employees on an at-will basis, were not conditional on any commitment by the employees to stay with CalAmp Corp.; nor were they conditioned on the performance of SR&ED tasks, the achievement of technical milestones, or the hours expended on eligible R&D projects. From a strict contract-law perspective, the employees had no legally enforceable right to require payment of the bonuses, which management represented to them as a gift, and the amounts were determined on the basis of years of service, current salary and merit, irrespective of whether a given employee's duties during the period involved experimental development, routine commercial production, quality assurance, or administrative work. Because the underlying reasons for the payment were the sharing of the financial success of the sale of the company and the purchaser's interest in favouring employee retention—rather than the execution of SR&ED—the Court concluded that no link existed between the expenditure and the SR&ED program.
2.3 The Pro-Rata Time-Allocation Fallacy and Proxy Salary Base Contamination

The dispute in CalAmp also exposed a pervasive methodological error in Canadian SR&ED claim preparation: the mechanical application of an employee's annual SR&ED time-allocation ratio to all forms of T4 employment income. When calculating the proxy salary base under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, claimants routinely determine the percentage of an employee's total working hours spent "directly engaged" in SR&ED (for example, 80% of 2,000 annual hours) and multiply that percentage against the employee's total T4 box 14 remuneration.

As the Tax Court's holding in CalAmp and the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy make clear, an amount can be allocated to SR&ED on a time basis only if there is a reasonable connection between that amount and the prosecution of SR&ED; the CRA policy passage relied upon by the Court states that a bonus paid out of income earned from a capital transaction, such as the sale of the business or of shares, does not have the capacity of being allocated to SR&ED, and that the allocation of salary or wages to SR&ED is made after such amounts are excluded from remuneration. When an employer introduces an extraordinary, non-recurring payment—such as a one-time post-acquisition incentive, a signing inducement, extended vacation or sick leave payout, a retiring allowance, or a stock option benefit—that payment cannot be blended into the general wage pool and prorated using regular timesheet percentages. Instead, each distinct category of remuneration must independently satisfy the threshold test of being incurred "on or in respect of" SR&ED. Including a non-SR&ED-linked lump-sum bonus in SR&ED salary or wages overstates the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and the resulting ITCs (as in CalAmp, where the inclusion of $1,990,036 in bonuses, compared with regular salaries of only $600,887 paid to the same SR&ED employees for the period, led to a $131,260 reduction of the refundable ITC), while bonuses are, in any event, excluded from the salary base used to compute the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR.
2.4 Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Documentation Linking Compensation to Technological Uncertainty and Systematic Experimentation

Beyond the character of the bonus itself, the taxpayer's evidentiary case failed to refute the Minister's assumptions of fact that the bonus incentives were not related to the prosecution of the SR&ED activities undertaken from March 1 to May 9, 2006, and that the extent and nature of those activities were in no way related to the payment of the bonuses. In Canadian SR&ED litigation, the burden of proof rests on the taxpayer to demolish the Minister's assumptions of fact by establishing, on a balance of probabilities, both the eligibility of the underlying technical work under subsection 248(1) and the direct linkage of the claimed financial expenditures under subsection 37(1) and subsection 37(8).

Under the CRA's administrative framework and Tax Court jurisprudence, proving that an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED requires contemporaneous evidence demonstrating hands-on involvement in carrying out experiments, tests, and analyses aimed at resolving a genuine technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved through standard practice or publicly available engineering knowledge. It similarly encompasses collecting data commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the experimentation and analyses, recording measurements, making calculations, preparing charts and graphs, or preparing computer programs integral to the experimental development. Furthermore, eligible direct engagement includes directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED activities being claimed in the year, while strictly excluding time spent by a manager or supervisor performing non-technological management or corporate decision-making activities.

In CalAmp, while the taxpayer declared fourteen SR&ED projects for the period, its only witness, its president Mr. Robert Rouleau, testified that the bonuses were calculated on the basis of years of service, current salary and merit, and candidly admitted that the bonuses paid to the SR&ED employees were not related to the prosecution of SR&ED activities undertaken during the two-month 2006 period, so that nothing in the record demonstrated that the bonuses were calculated, awarded, or earned based on the employees' technical contributions to those experimental activities. Without evidence showing that the bonus rewarded specific experimental development tasks or the resolution of technological uncertainties during the taxation year, the Court found that the payment was an isolated event rather than the result of Old Dataradio's traditional bonus policy or of a recurrent need to compensate employees engaged in SR&ED (applying Alcatel Canada Inc. v. Canada, 2006 TCC 149), and that the appellant had not shown the expenditures to have a direct relationship with the research projects and to be essential to their completion (citing Laboratoire Du-Var Inc. v. Canada, 2012 TCC 366).
2.5 Second- and Third-Order Jurisprudential Implications for Corporate M&A and SR&ED Governance

The decision in CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. carries profound second- and third-order implications for technology mergers and acquisitions, corporate restructurings, and technical compensation design in Canada. From a corporate transaction perspective, an acquisition of control of a Canadian corporation automatically triggers a deemed taxation year-end under subsection 249(4) of the ITA and constitutes a "loss restriction event" under subsection 251.2(2) (a concept introduced into the ITA in 2013, after the 2006 transaction at issue; in CalAmp itself, Old Dataradio, which had already changed its year-end from July 31 to February 28 to match that of the purchaser, had a second 2006 taxation year that ended on May 9, 2006, the date of the acquisition, and ceased to be a Canadian-controlled private corporation on May 10, 2006). Moreover, when a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) is acquired by a non-resident public corporation—such as CalAmp Corp., a US publicly traded entity—the Canadian subsidiary immediately loses its CCPC status, reducing its federal SR&ED ITC rate from the enhanced 35% refundable rate to the 15% non-refundable rate and subjecting pre-acquisition ITC carryforwards to strict streaming rules under subsections 127(9.1) and 127(9.2). When transaction planners attempt to offset these structural tax costs by claiming SR&ED ITCs on post-closing retention or deal bonuses, CalAmp illustrates that such bonuses will be disallowed where, as a question of fact, the underlying reasons for their payment relate to the transaction rather than to the prosecution of SR&ED in the taxation year.

In addition, CalAmp also addressed timing: the Court held that the word "year" in subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) refers to the taxation year, which here corresponds to the appellant's fiscal period from March 1 to May 9, 2006 under sections 249 and 249.1 of the ITA, and that this is the only period relevant to determining whether the bonuses (accrued as of the closing date and paid no earlier than June 23, 2006) were related to the prosecution of SR&ED, a nexus inquiry distinct from the timing rules of section 5 and subsection 78(4) of the ITA and the general rules of section 37. Even where a bonus is accrued in a taxation year and paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year so as to satisfy subsection 78(4) of the ITA for general business deductibility under section 9, compliance with subsection 78(4) would not, on the reasoning in CalAmp, cure a lack of nexus under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), although the Court did not itself address subsection 78(4). Timing compliance and employment tax inclusion are necessary prerequisites, but they remain legally insufficient conditions for SR&ED eligibility.

Consequently, the ruling supports heightened CRA audit scrutiny of variable compensation across Canada. Drawing on CalAmp, the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy and subsequent jurisprudence such as Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 183 (which considered whether remuneration paid to a research head based on net sales of new products was a "bonus" excluded from the salary base under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, and held that it was not), CRA SR&ED Financial Reviewers may demand employment contracts, bonus plan texts, board of directors' compensation resolutions, and M&A share purchase agreements whenever an SR&ED claim displays a year-over-year spike in T4 salary bases relative to headcount. Any variable pay lacking explicit, documented performance criteria tied to daily experimental duties is systematically carved out of the SR&ED salary base prior to applying the employee's SR&ED time-allocation percentage.
3. Comparative Summary Table: Statutory Requirements, Taxpayer Failures, and Judicial Standards of Proof

The following table maps each governing statutory and regulatory requirement examined in CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 201 (and the related CRA Salary or Wages Policy) against the taxpayer's specific legal and evidentiary failures and the standard of proof mandated by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in CalAmp (2013 TCC 201)
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Threshold

cells: ITA Subsection 248(1) & Section 5 (Definition of "Salary or Wages")

Remuneration must constitute income from an office or employment computed under sections 5 to 8 of the ITA (including base salary, wages, and bona fide employment bonuses), excluding non-eligible items such as stock option benefits or retiring allowances.

The taxpayer assumed that satisfying the subsection 248(1) / section 5 definition of employment income was sufficient, in and of itself, to render the one-time bonus eligible for pro-rata SR&ED allocation.

Threshold Prerequisite Only: Proving that a payment is taxable under section 5 on an employee's T4 slip satisfies only the threshold classification of "salary or wages"; the taxpayer must still independently prove the purposive SR&ED nexus under section 37.
ITA Paragraph 37(1)(a) (Expenditures "On" or "In Respect Of" SR&ED)
Current expenditures must be incurred "on" or "in respect of" SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer.

The bonus incentives were paid mainly so that employees could share in the financial success of the sale of the company and to favour employee retention for the purchaser, rather than for the execution of SR&ED, resulting in a complete absence of a causal or functional link to SR&ED.

Direct Causal / Functional Nexus: Even though "in respect of" has wide scope, the taxpayer must establish on a balance of probabilities a reasonable connection between the specific payment and the prosecution of SR&ED, determined as a question of fact by reference to the underlying reasons for paying it (as distinct from the method used to calculate it).
ITA Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) (Proxy Method: "Directly Engaged" & Reasonable Relation)

Under the proxy method, eligible salary or wages are restricted to employees "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada, and limited strictly to "that portion of an expenditure... for salary or wages of an employee who is directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada that can reasonably be considered to relate to such work having regard to the time spent by the employee thereon".

The taxpayer included the full $1,990,036 in bonuses paid to its employees directly engaged in SR&ED in its claimed salary or wages, alongside regular salaries of only $600,887 for the period, despite the bonus not representing consideration for hours spent directly engaged in SR&ED.

Task-Specific Consideration Proof: The taxpayer must demonstrate through employment contracts, bonus plans, and timesheets that the specific payment was earned by virtue of performing hands-on SR&ED tasks during the taxation year.
ITA Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) (Traditional Method: Directly Undertaking, Supervising, or Supporting)

Under the traditional method, salary or wages must be paid to employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting the prosecution of SR&ED, to the extent the amount reasonably relates to such work (excluding non-technological management).

Not directly at issue, as the appellant elected the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA; in any event, the bonuses were determined by years of service, current salary and merit, irrespective of whether their specific hours involved hands-on experimentation, technical supervision, or non-eligible commercial/administrative integration duties.

Granular Activity Segregation: The taxpayer must segregate eligible technical supervision and experimentation from non-technological management, corporate integration, and commercial duties, proving the remuneration compensates only the former.
ITR Subsections 2900(4) & 2900(9) (Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base)

The proxy salary base used to compute notional overhead (PPA) must include only eligible directly engaged salary or wages under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), subject to statutory caps and exclusions, including the exclusion under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR of all bonuses and remuneration based on profits.

The judgment did not separately address the PPA; the dispute concerned the inclusion of the $1,990,036 in bonuses in SR&ED salary or wages under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), which the Minister disallowed, reducing the refundable ITC by $131,260 (bonuses being, in any event, excluded from the PPA salary base).

Uncontaminated Base Verification: Every component of remuneration entering the subsection 2900(4) base must be audited and verified as consideration for direct SR&ED engagement before the proxy multiplier is applied.
ITA Subsection 248(1) (Substantive SR&ED Eligibility & Contemporaneous Evidence)
The underlying work must resolve technological uncertainty through systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis, supported by contemporaneous technical and labour records.

While the company declared fourteen SR&ED projects, its only witness admitted that the bonuses were not related to the prosecution of SR&ED during the period, and it did not refute the Minister's assumptions that the bonuses were unrelated to the extent and nature of its SR&ED activities.

Integrated Technical-Financial Trail: Contemporaneous project records (test logs, commits, engineering notes, and technical performance evaluations) must cross-reference and substantiate the financial basis of incentive remuneration.

body.text: 4. Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their legal and technical advisors can proactively structure operations to avoid the disallowances crystallized in CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 201, the following two applied industry case studies analyze high-risk scenarios and provide step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, technical documentation, contract drafting, and experimentation tracking.
4.1 Case Study 1: Post-Acquisition RF Telemetry and Embedded Firmware Experimental Development
Scenario and Pitfall Profile

AeroWave Telemetry Canada Inc. ("AeroWave"), a Montreal-based developer of industrial ultra-narrowband (UNB) radio frequency (RF) transceivers and embedded mesh-networking firmware, is acquired mid-year by a publicly traded multinational telecommunications conglomerate. Following the acquisition of control (which triggers a deemed taxation year-end under subsection 249(4) of the ITA), the parent company wishes to establish a $600,000 incentive pool for AeroWave's 12 senior RF hardware and embedded firmware engineers to prevent attrition and accelerate the development of a next-generation cognitive radio transceiver.

The core engineering project seeks to resolve a genuine technological uncertainty: existing UNB transceiver architectures suffer from catastrophic phase-noise degradation and packet collisions when operating simultaneously across sub-GHz unlicensed bands in high-multipath metallic industrial environments, and standard Digital Signal Processing (DSP) adaptive filtering algorithms exceed the thermal and 15 mW power budget of the target ARM Cortex-M microcontroller. AeroWave's human resources department initially drafts a "Post-Merger Retention Bonus Agreement" granting each engineer a one-time $50,000 lump-sum payment payable 12 months after the share purchase closing date, conditional solely on the engineer not voluntarily resigning prior to that date. AeroWave elects the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA and intends to claim 85% of the $600,000 bonus pool ($510,000) as eligible SR&ED salary and wages based on the engineers' average 85% time allocation to SR&ED projects. Under CalAmp, 2013 TCC 201, the CRA will disallow 100% of the $510,000 bonus claim (bonuses being, in any event, excluded from the salary base used to compute the Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR) because the payment is triggered by the acquisition of control and passive retention rather than the active performance of SR&ED.
Step 1: Restructuring Contractual Terms and Eliminating Transaction and Retention Triggers

To satisfy paragraph 37(1)(a) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) of the ITA, legal counsel must completely abandon the standalone "Post-Merger Retention Agreement" and instead integrate the variable compensation into an amended Annual Employment and Technical Performance Compensation Schedule under each engineer's core employment contract. All references to the share purchase agreement, change of control, and passive "stay-until-date" retention conditions must be excised from the contractual text. In their place, the employment contract addendum must stipulate that the variable remuneration constitutes performance-based employment salary earned directly as consideration for the employee's ongoing technical services rendered during the taxation year.

Specifically, the contract must condition entitlement to, and quantification of, the variable pay on two objective operational metrics: first, the verified hours the engineer spends directly engaged in executing assigned experimental development work packages during the fiscal period; and second, the completion of rigorous technical investigation cycles—specifically formulating hypotheses, executing RF chamber and field tests, and analyzing DSP algorithm performance metrics—irrespective of whether the technological uncertainty is ultimately resolved or whether the commercial product succeeds. Conditioning bonus vesting on systematic experimental effort and analytical rigour rather than commercial product launch or passive tenure preserves SR&ED eligibility while aligning with the legal definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1). Furthermore, the contract must mandate that any accrued variable remuneration for a taxation year (including a short taxation year triggered by subsection 249(4)) be unconditionally paid within 175 days following the taxation year-end, ensuring strict compliance with the 180-day payment rule in subsection 78(4) of the ITA.
Step 2: Restructuring Project Governance and Separating Non-Technological Management

Post-acquisition environments frequently require senior engineers and team leads to participate in corporate integration committees, IT migration, supply-chain harmonization, and commercial product roadmapping. Under the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy (section 7.1), consistent with CalAmp, time spent by a manager or supervisor performing non-technological management activities or corporate decision-making is strictly excluded from SR&ED. Consequently, AeroWave must establish a formal SR&ED Technical Governance Charter that separates corporate post-merger integration from experimental development. For the two Engineering Directors who both supervise the RF lab and sit on the parent company's integration steering committee, governance protocols must split their work into two distinct cost centres: Cost Centre 100 for Corporate and Commercial Integration (ineligible) and Cost Centre 200 for Direct SR&ED Technical Direction. Only hours logged in Cost Centre 200—where the directors actively direct the technical course of ongoing SR&ED experiments, review spectrum analyzer phase-noise plots, and modify DSP filter architectures—are eligible for inclusion in the subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) proxy salary base.
Step 3: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Prove Technological Uncertainty and Systematic Experimentation

To ensure that the performance-based variable pay is unimpeachably linked to eligible SR&ED under subsection 248(1), AeroWave must implement a structured technical documentation protocol mapping each engineer's compensation evaluation directly to experimental outputs. At the inception of the taxation year, the lead architect must compile a Technological Baseline and Uncertainty Dossier documenting why standard IEEE 802.15.4g protocols and textbook Kalman or Least Mean Squares (LMS) adaptive filters fail to maintain a Bit Error Rate (BER) below 10−5 under −118 dBm sensitivity within a 15 mW power envelope.

Throughout the year, each experimental cycle must be recorded in an immutable Jira/Confluence and Git repository structure that captures the specific hypothesis under test (for example, testing whether a fixed-point quantized polyphase decimation filter with dynamic phase-locked loop bandwidth switching reduces adjacent-channel phase noise by 12 dB while reducing MCU clock cycles by 35%), the experimental protocol and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test bench setup, the raw empirical data including oscilloscope power traces, vector network analyzer S-parameters, and BER logs, and the technical conclusions explaining why the hypothesis succeeded or failed. At the close of the assessment period, each engineer's formal written performance evaluation—which legally authorizes the payout of their variable remuneration—must explicitly cite the specific Jira experimental epics, Git commit hashes, and technical analysis reports authored by that engineer during the year.
Step 4: Experimentation Time-Tracking and Uncontaminated Proxy Base Calculation

Instead of applying an arbitrary year-end percentage estimate across all T4 earnings, AeroWave must deploy a bi-weekly contemporaneous time-tracking system signed off by the Technical Director. Engineers must log hours daily across four mutually exclusive activity codes: SR-EXP for hands-on experimental development such as DSP coding, RF board prototyping, chamber testing, and empirical data analysis (eligible under both the proxy and traditional methods); SR-SUP for technical support work commensurate with and directly in support of SR&ED (eligible under the proxy method if performed by directly engaged staff and under the traditional method); ENG-STD for routine commercial engineering, customer firmware customization, and regulatory certification testing (ineligible); and CORP-INT for post-acquisition administrative meetings, HR training, and non-technological management (ineligible). Because the variable performance pay is contractually earned across active engineering duties based on documented quarterly performance reviews, and any one-off signing or transaction inducement is isolated in a separate payroll code (IND-NON-SRED) that is 100% excluded from the SR&ED claim, AeroWave establishes a transparent, audit-proof nexus between the claimed remuneration and the hours directly engaged in SR&ED.
4.2 Case Study 2: Shop-Floor Advanced Materials and Automated Process Engineering
Scenario and Pitfall Profile

Nordic Composite Structures Ltd. ("Nordic"), an Ontario-based Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) manufacturing structural thermoplastic composite components for the aerospace and heavy transportation sectors, undertakes an ambitious shop-floor experimental development project. Nordic seeks to develop a continuous, high-speed automated induction-welding and in-situ consolidation process for carbon-fibre-reinforced polyetheretherketone (CF/PEEK) laminates. The technological uncertainty centres on the coupled electromagnetic-thermal-crystallinity dynamics at feed rates exceeding 4.0 metres per minute: eddy-current crowding at the laminate edges causes localized polymer degradation (> 420°C), while rapid cooling in the core region suppresses PEEK crystallinity below the mandatory 28% threshold required for structural interlaminar shear strength. Resolving this uncertainty requires custom induction coil geometry design, closed-loop pyrometric thermal feedback algorithms, and destructive shop-floor experimental trials involving both specialized polymer engineers and non-specialized shop-floor CNC and robotics technicians.

In preparing its SR&ED claim, Nordic encounters three severe legal pitfalls under CalAmp and the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy. First, following a major commercial supply contract award and a minority equity recapitalization, Nordic pays its shop-floor technicians and R&D engineers a "Special Milestone & Plant Retention Bonus" calculated primarily on overall plant commercial output targets and employee tenure, alongside a cash payout for unused extended vacation leave. Second, Nordic includes a $120,000 discretionary bonus paid to its Chief Technology Officer—who owns 15% of the issued shares of Nordic, rendering the CTO a "specified employee" under subsection 248(1) of the ITA—in its SR&ED expenditure pool. Third, Nordic claims 50% of the annual wages and bonuses of 10 non-specialized shop-floor machine operators under the proxy method without contemporaneous supervision logs or segregation between commercial production runs and experimental trial runs. Under CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc., 2013 TCC 201 (read together with the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy and later jurisprudence on remuneration and the salary base, such as Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc., 2016 TCC 183), the CRA will disallow the plant retention and commercial output bonus for lacking a direct nexus to SR&ED, disallow the extended vacation payouts as non-engaged time, disallow the CTO's bonus due to the statutory prohibition on bonuses or remuneration based on profits for specified employees, and disallow the shop-floor operators' wages due to lack of proof of direct engagement and scientific or technological supervision.
Step 1: Restructuring Compensation Contracts for Specified Employees, Engineers, and Shop-Floor Technicians

To comply with subsection 37(1), subsection 37(8), and section 2900 of the ITR, Nordic must overhaul its compensation architecture across its three distinct employee tiers. For Tier A, comprising specified employees (specifically the CTO holding 15% of the corporation's shares), subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines a "specified employee" as an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), subsection 37(9), and subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, no bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee may be included in SR&ED expenditures or the proxy salary base, and their eligible base salary is capped at 5× the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, prorated for the number of days in the year on which the individual is a specified employee (with the SR&ED portion then determined by reference to the time spent directly engaged in SR&ED); for the subsection 2900(4) proxy salary base, subsection 2900(7) of the ITR further limits a specified employee's salary or wages to the lesser of 75% of that employee's salary or wages for the year and 2.5× the YMPE, prorated for the days employed in the year. Consequently, Nordic must amend the CTO's employment contract to eliminate the discretionary bonus and replace it with an increased regular base salary paid through regular bi-weekly payroll in direct consideration of the CTO's hands-on technical experimentation and supervision duties, while capping the SR&ED claim for the CTO at the statutory 5× limit prorated by documented SR&ED hours.

For Tier B, comprising non-specified specialized polymer and robotics engineers, Nordic must split its variable pay plan into two legally separate instruments: a Commercial Plant Output Plan (explicitly excluded 100% from SR&ED claims) and an SR&ED Technical Investigation Compensation Plan. The latter must contractually link variable remuneration strictly to the execution of experimental work packages on the CF/PEEK induction-welding line, such as designing multi-turn flux-concentrator coils, executing factorial Design of Experiments (DoE) runs, and performing Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) crystallinity analyses. For Tier C, comprising non-specialized shop-floor technicians, section 7.1.1 of the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy dictates that non-specialized employees can be considered "directly engaged in SR&ED" only when their hands-on work is directly in support of and an integral part of the experimental development, and is supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. Their hourly employment contracts and shift assignments must explicitly define "Experimental Trial Shifts" as distinct technical duties compensated through regular hourly wages, while excluding extended vacation payouts, sick-leave cash-outs, and general plant retention bonuses from the SR&ED wage calculation.
Step 2: Restructuring Shop-Floor Governance and Supervision Protocols

Because shop-floor SR&ED takes place in an industrial facility that also houses commercial manufacturing, Nordic must institute strict physical and operational governance to satisfy section 13.5.4 (Shop floor SR&ED) and section 7.1.1 (Non-specialized employees) of the CRA's Salary or Wages Policy. Whenever the automated induction-welding line is transitioned from commercial manufacturing to SR&ED experimentation, an Experimental Work Order (EWO) must be issued in the Manufacturing Execution System (MES) under a formal Experimental Cell Lockout Protocol. During an active EWO, commercial production is halted on that line, raw CF/PEEK prepreg consumed is tagged as experimental trial material, and commercial cost-of-goods-sold (COGS) accounting is suspended. Furthermore, every EWO assigned to non-specialized CNC and robotics technicians must designate a supervising Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) or Ph.D. Polymer Scientist. The supervisor must issue written experimental setup parameters prior to the shift, remain actively involved in directing the trial run, and sign off on the technician's experimental data sheet and time log at the conclusion of the shift.
Step 3: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Substantiate Systematic Investigation

To ensure that every hour and dollar claimed under the EWOs withstands a Joint CRA Technical and Financial Review, Nordic must maintain a centralized Shop-Floor SR&ED Evidence Binder. Within this binder, every EWO must incorporate a Quantitative Hypothesis Matrix stating the exact technological variable under investigation—for example, evaluating under EWO-2026-04 whether a dual-frequency (150 kHz/450 kHz) split-capacitor induction coil with active nitrogen vortex cooling reduces the edge-to-centre thermal gradient ΔT from 68°C to < 15°C at a consolidation speed of 4.5 m/min. Each EWO record must be paired with contemporaneous empirical measurement logs, including infrared thermography datasets, ultrasonic C-scan void-content maps, DSC crystallinity curves, and short-beam shear test failure loads recorded by the technicians and analyzed by the polymer engineers during each experimental run.
Step 4: Precision Experimentation Time-Tracking and Payroll Segregation

To prevent the pro-rata contamination error that proved fatal in CalAmp, Nordic must configure its enterprise resource planning (ERP) and payroll systems to segregate eligible and ineligible remuneration at the source in accordance with the following structured accounting matrix:

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis and Compliance Imperatives for Canadian SR&ED Claimants

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 201 stands as the definitive Canadian authority governing the nexus required between employee compensation and Scientific Research and Experimental Development. The ruling establishes that the broad inclusion of bonuses and incentives within "salary or wages" under subsection 248(1) and section 5 of the Income Tax Act is merely a gateway condition. To qualify as a deductible SR&ED expenditure under subsection 37(1) and enter the proxy or traditional salary base under subsection 37(8) and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, the taxpayer bears the burden of proving that the specific payment was incurred "on or in respect of" the prosecution of SR&ED and that the portion claimed "can reasonably be considered to relate to such work having regard to the time spent by the employee thereon", which, as a question of fact, turns on the underlying reasons for paying it.

When corporations undergo mergers, acquisitions of control, or internal restructurings, any one-time bonus, retention incentive, or transaction payment triggered by the corporate event rather than the execution of experimental development is legally severed from the SR&ED regime—even when paid to full-time R&D scientists and engineers. By proactively structuring employment agreements to tie variable compensation directly to documented experimental workflows, isolating non-technological management and commercial duties, adhering strictly to specified employee restrictions, and maintaining contemporaneous time-tracking linked to technical evidence, Canadian taxpayers can insulate their SR&ED claims from reassessment and fully realize the statutory incentives under sections 37 and 127 of the Income Tax Act.

outcome: Appeal allowed in part; court determined specific engineering projects met SR&ED criteria while others were routine.
